equivalents.note: The Tibetan translates the rāga name by sense, 'the one that makes joyful', instead of transcribing it.

equivalents.wylie: mtshan nyid med la mtshon du med
equivalents.note: The Tibetan splits the compound into two clauses, 'it has no characteristics and cannot be pointed to', with no separate word for na jāi, 'does not go'; the comment (cp.15.m2) has only mtshan nyid med pa la sogs pa for alakṣyalakṣaṇādi.
rang bzhin, usually the word for svabhāva, here renders sarua (svarūpa); the comment uses rang bzhin for svarūpa in cp.15.m2 but ngo bo nyid in cp.15.m4.

The Tibetan has 'their road went elsewhere' (de yi lam ni gzhan du song), as if reading āna, 'other', with bāṭa, 'road'; Munidatta's anāvarta at this point is phyir mi ldog pa, 'not turning back', in the Tibetan comment (cp.15.m2).

The Tibetan verse puts 'body' (lus kyi ngo bo, 'the nature of the body') where the Bengali has kula, in line with Munidatta's gloss kule pratyekaśarīre, 'in each body', while the comment (cp.15.m3) transcribes the word as ku la and glosses it rang gi lus.

The Tibetan turns the vocative 'O fool' into a genitive, 'the deluded one's straight road' (rmongs pa'i lam drang), though its comment keeps the vocative kye'i rmongs pa (cp.15.m3, cp.15.m5); rmongs pa also renders moha.

equivalents.wylie: rgyal po yi ni gser lam
equivalents.note: The Tibetan has 'the king's golden road', apparently taking 'golden' (gser) from the following kaṇḍhārā, and ends the line with log, 'wrong' or 'turned back', whose source in the Bengali is unclear.

The Tibetan has gser, 'gold', in 'the king's golden road', as if kaṇḍhārā held kanaka, 'gold'; its comment renders Munidatta's kanakapathadhārayā as gser gyi lam bzung nas, 'keeping to the golden road' (cp.15.m3).
The Tibetan has mtha' dang gting, 'the end and the bottom', so it takes thāhā here as 'bottom', where in song 5 it had 'dug gnas, 'place to stay'.
skyal rdzas is literally 'ferrying gear'; the comment (cp.15.m4) instead has rkyal, 'float', in gru rkyal.
The Tibetan has lam 'phrang, 'narrow pass', for the two roads, which it calls south and north (lho byang) where the Bengali has left and right.

The Tibetan has 'go on the road known by the eye' (mig gis shes pa'i lam) where the Bengali has going the road with eyes closed (ākhi bujia), perhaps reading bujia as 'understood' (bujh-) rather than 'closed' (buj-).
The Tibetan line names three posts, khral sa, sho gam and 'gag ('barrier'), and its comment (cp.15.m6) four ('gag, khral sa, sho gam, 'phrang) for Munidatta's ghaṭakuṭī, gulma and dālaka.
The Tibetan has rdzing bu'i tshal, 'grove of the pool', not chu skyes tshal, 'lotus grove', which fits a text reading sarasi vane without the -ja that Shastri restores in śarasi[ja]vane.
Here the comment renders mārga as plain lam (thabs lam, lam gzhan, rdo rje'i lam, a wa d+hU tI'i lam), as in cp.15.m5 and cp.15.m6, whereas mārgavara in cp.15.m2 is lam mchog.
In Virūpa's verse the Tibetan has nyi zlar, 'to sun and moon', for candrārka, 'moon and sun', reversing the order.

questions: yuganaddha (cp.15.m6): not matched. Where the Sanskrit has stabdhonmīlitalocane yuganaddhaṃ paśyati, the Tibetan has mig zim bu mi g.yo ba'i mig zung gis yang dag par mthong, 'sees rightly with the pair of eyes half-closed and unmoving', with no zung 'jug. mig zung seems to render the dual locane and yang dag par to stand where yuganaddhaṃ is, so either the translators' manuscript read something else (samyak?) or zung is meant to carry yuga. Please decide whether this counts as a witness difference.

rājapatha and kaṇḍhārā (cp.15.2b) share one Tibetan phrase, rgyal po yi ni gser lam. I gave the whole phrase for rajapatha and gser alone for kandhara, so the two scripts overlap. The closing log is not accounted for; it may render ṇa bhulaha, 'do not stray', which ma yo in the first half already seems to cover.
